title: HLA-B Polymorphism, Bw4/Bw6 Public Epitopes, and Current versus Historic Serum
summary: Why HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene, how the mutually exclusive Bw4 and Bw6 public epitopes at residues 77–83 turn one alloantibody into a broad single-antigen-bead pattern, and why only a positive crossmatch on current recipient serum vetoes a renal transplant.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 50 Hit 7 (HLA-B as the most polymorphic HLA gene and the allele counts), Hit 14 (Bw4/Bw6 as a diallelic public-epitope system and public-epitope cross-reactivity) and Trap 6 (current vs historic serum crossmatch). Checked against Barker 2026, Robinson 2020, Di 2021, Arumugam 2024, Gumperz 1995, El-Awar 2017, Bang 2025, Althaf 2017 and Katalinić 2025. Hit 7’s 2019 counts are outdated (register rv-hla-allele-counts-2019) and Hit 14 calls Bw4/Bw6 an HLA-B system although Bw4 is also carried by HLA-A23, A24, A25 and A32 (register rv-bw4-also-hla-a); Hit 14’s “80–90% of posttransplant kidney alloantibodies target CREG determinants” traces to a closed-access 1994 paper and is taught as pending (register rv-creg-80-90-source); Trap 6’s one-line grading of historic positivity is incomplete (register rv-historic-xm-risk-grade). Not taught: the Number Vault rows, the chapter figure, HLA-B leader matching, KIR genotyping, eplet-level matching algorithms, desensitisation protocols.

objectives: Explain why HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene and why any printed allele count is a database snapshot.
Describe Bw4 and Bw6 as mutually exclusive public epitopes defined by residues 77–83, and predict the broad single-antigen-bead pattern a public-epitope antibody produces.
Separate a positive CDC crossmatch on current recipient serum, which vetoes renal transplantation, from a positive crossmatch on historic serum, which is graded as immunological risk.

scenes.title: One antibody, twenty beads
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. A kidney transplant candidate has three serum results on file: a serum from three years ago that gave a positive T-cell CDC crossmatch against a previous donor; today’s serum, which is CDC-crossmatch negative against the new donor; and a single-antigen-bead panel in which a whole family of HLA-B antigens is positive together with HLA-A23 and A24. Question token: “One shared epitope or twenty antibodies — and does the old positive still veto the transplant?”

cues.text: Invented case. A kidney transplant candidate has three results on file. A serum from three years ago gave a positive T-cell crossmatch against an earlier donor.
Today’s serum is crossmatch negative against the new donor. But the single-antigen beads light up a whole family of HLA-B antigens, plus HLA-A23 and A24.
Is that one shared epitope or twenty separate antibodies? And does the old positive still veto the transplant?

props.label: One shared epitope, or twenty antibodies?

scenes.title: Why HLA-B is the biggest book
scenes.altText: Polymorphism cards (Barker 2026; Robinson 2020; Di 2021; Arumugam 2024). The HLA genes sit in the extended MHC, which spans more than 7 Mb of chromosome 6p21.3 and holds over 420 genes; they are the most polymorphic genes in the human genome and are described as hyperpolymorphic. Among them HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene: by the December 2020 IPD-IMGT/HLA release more than 7,000 alleles were named for HLA-B against about 6,000 each for HLA-A and HLA-C. The database total keeps climbing: over 25,000 alleles for 45 genes in October 2019, over 35,000 in 2022, and more than 43,000 alleles from 47 genes by July 2025 — so any printed allele count is a snapshot. Six classical genes (HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQB1, -DPB1) account for 87.3% of all named alleles, and estimates suggest roughly 3 million alleles per class I locus may exist in people.

cues.text: The HLA genes sit in the extended major histocompatibility complex, more than seven megabases of chromosome 6p21.3 holding over four hundred and twenty genes. They are the most polymorphic genes in the human genome.
Among them, HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene. By the December 2020 database release more than seven thousand alleles were named for HLA-B, against about six thousand each for HLA-A and HLA-C.

The totals keep climbing. Over twenty-five thousand alleles for forty-five genes in October 2019, over thirty-five thousand in 2022, and more than forty-three thousand from forty-seven genes by July 2025.

So any printed allele count is a snapshot, not a constant. Six classical genes carry eighty-seven point three percent of all named alleles, and estimates put perhaps three million alleles per class I locus out in the population.

scenes.title: Bw4 and Bw6: the shared cover
scenes.altText: Public-epitope cards (Gumperz 1995; El-Awar 2017). Every HLA-B allele carries one of two mutually exclusive serological epitopes, Bw4 or Bw6: Bw6 on roughly two-thirds of HLA-B alleles, Bw4 on the remaining third. The residues that form them map to positions 77–83 of the class I heavy chain; alleles differing only in that stretch (B*15:02 is Bw6, B*15:13 is Bw4) switch epitope. Bw4 and Bw6 were first taken for two HLA-B antigens and later recognised as determinants shared across a large family of alleles — a PUBLIC epitope, as opposed to a PRIVATE epitope found on one antigen only. Public epitopes are what cross-reactivity, historically described as cross-reactive groups (CREGs), actually is: one antibody binds every antigen carrying the shared epitope. Bw6 is found only on HLA-B; Bw4 is found on HLA-B AND on some HLA-A antigens — A23, A24, A25 and A32 — with the Bw4-associated epitope defined by leucine 82 or arginine 83 in the α1 domain of the class I heavy chain. Bw6 alleles are invariant across 77–83 with the single exception of B*73:01. Bw4 is also the ligand recognised by the NK-cell receptor NKB1 (KIR3DL1).

cues.text: Every HLA-B allele carries one of two mutually exclusive serological epitopes, Bw4 or Bw6. Bw6 sits on about two-thirds of HLA-B alleles, Bw4 on the remaining third. The residues that form them map to positions seventy-seven to eighty-three of the class one heavy chain.

They were first taken for two HLA-B antigens, then recognised as determinants shared across a whole family of alleles. That is a public epitope, as opposed to a private epitope found on one antigen only.
Public epitopes are what cross-reactivity really is. The old cross-reactive groups, the CREGs, are one antibody binding every antigen that carries the shared epitope.

And the system is not purely HLA-B. Bw6 is found only on HLA-B, but Bw4 is also carried by HLA-A23, A24, A25 and A32, defined by leucine eighty-two or arginine eighty-three in the alpha one domain. Bw4 is also the ligand for the natural killer receptor NKB1.

scenes.title: Reading the three results
scenes.altText: Decision cards. (1) The broad bead pattern: one antibody against a public epitope turns every bead carrying that epitope positive, so a wide single-antigen-bead pattern spanning many HLA-B antigens plus A23 and A24 fits ONE anti-Bw4 specificity rather than twenty antibodies (El-Awar 2017; Gumperz 1995). (2) Anti-Bw4 is not harmless: in a published case a low-risk recipient with a negative pre-transplant screen developed de novo donor-specific antibodies to B58 and B59 on Bw4-bearing beads, with C4d-positive peritubular capillaritis and active antibody-mediated rejection by postoperative day 9, treated with plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulin and rituximab; the authors note anti-Bw4 and anti-Bw6 are generally not treated as rejection risk factors yet can be causative (Bang 2025). (3) Serum timing: a positive CDC crossmatch using CURRENT serum with IgG class I donor-specific antibody is graded high risk — hyperacute rejection, a veto to transplantation. A positive CDC crossmatch on HISTORICAL serum is graded by antibody class and specificity, not automatically vetoed; historical positives caused by cross-reactive alloantibodies are intermediate risk (Althaf 2017). Every positive crossmatch, fresh or historical, was once a contraindication; later work showed a historical positive did not significantly affect outcome when the fresh-serum crossmatch was negative (Katalinić 2025). A serum older than six months cannot predict the crossmatch, so a virtual crossmatch needs a sample from within three to six months (Althaf 2017).

cues.text: Score our case. The broad bead pattern first. One antibody against a public epitope turns every bead carrying it positive, so a wide pattern across HLA-B plus A23 and A24 fits one anti-Bw4 specificity, not twenty antibodies.

That is not a harmless finding. In a published case a low-risk recipient developed donor-specific antibodies to B58 and B59 on Bw4 beads, with C4d-positive capillaritis and antibody-mediated rejection by day nine.
Now the serum timing. A positive crossmatch on current serum with IgG class one donor-specific antibody is the high-risk result: hyperacute rejection, a veto to transplantation.

A positive crossmatch on historical serum is graded by antibody class and specificity instead, and is not an automatic veto when the current crossmatch is negative. But a serum older than six months cannot predict the crossmatch, so a virtual crossmatch needs a sample from the last three to six months.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “An old positive crossmatch vetoes the transplant just like a current one” (✓ only a positive crossmatch on CURRENT serum is the veto; a historical positive is graded by antibody class and specificity); “Twenty positive beads means twenty antibodies” (✓ one antibody to a public epitope such as Bw4 turns every bead carrying it positive); “Bw4 and Bw6 are carried only by HLA-B” (✓ Bw6 yes, but Bw4 is also carried by HLA-A23, A24, A25 and A32).

cues.text: Trap one: an old positive crossmatch vetoes the transplant just like a current one. No. Only a positive crossmatch on current serum is the veto; a historical positive is graded by antibody class and specificity.
Trap two: twenty positive beads means twenty antibodies. No. One antibody against a public epitope such as Bw4 turns every bead carrying it positive.
Trap three: Bw4 and Bw6 are carried only by HLA-B. Bw6 yes, but Bw4 is also carried by HLA-A23, A24, A25 and A32.

cues.text: Memory aid. B is the biggest book: HLA-B has more named alleles than any other HLA gene. Bw4 and Bw6 are the cover whole families of antigens share, so one antibody reads every copy. And only today’s serum can veto the transplant.

Where it breaks: the biggest-book ranking is a snapshot of a database that grows every quarter, and allele counts are not the same as functional diversity; the shared-cover image hides that Bw4 is also on some HLA-A antigens while Bw6 is HLA-B only; and today’s-serum-only does not mean a historical positive is harmless, because it is still graded as immunological risk.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “HLA-B = most polymorphic HLA gene · > 7,000 alleles (Dec 2020) · database > 43,000 alleles (Jul 2025)”, “Bw4/Bw6 = mutually exclusive public epitopes at residues 77–83 · only CURRENT-serum CDC positivity vetoes the transplant”.

cues.text: HLA-B carries more named alleles than any other HLA gene, its mutually exclusive Bw4 and Bw6 public epitopes let one alloantibody light up a whole family of antigens, and only a positive complement-dependent cytotoxicity crossmatch using current recipient serum is the absolute veto to renal transplantation.

props.label: HLA-B = most polymorphic HLA gene · counts are a moving snapshot
Bw4/Bw6 public epitopes at 77–83 · only CURRENT serum vetoes

explanation.what: Plain language: the HLA molecules on your cells come in enormous numbers of versions, and HLA-B has more versions than any other HLA gene. Some of the shapes antibodies recognise are shared by many different HLA types, so one antibody can react with a long list of them. Before a kidney transplant the lab mixes recipient serum with donor cells; whether a positive result stops the transplant depends on how fresh that serum is. Scientific terms: major histocompatibility complex (MHC), IPD-IMGT/HLA Database, allele, public epitope, private epitope, cross-reactive group (CREG), Bw4, Bw6, single-antigen bead (SAB), donor-specific antibody (DSA), complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) crossmatch, antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR), virtual crossmatch.
explanation.why: Balancing selection on peptide presentation has driven HLA class I genes to extreme allelic diversity, and HLA-B leads. Because many alleles share the same surface stretch at residues 77–83, antibodies raised against one antigen bind every antigen carrying that shared stretch — the classical CREG phenomenon. Antibody titres and specificities drift over time, so a serum drawn years ago describes a past immune state, not the one that will meet the graft today.
explanation.measure: IPD-IMGT/HLA: >25,000 alleles across 45 genes (Oct 2019), >35,000 (2022), >43,000 across 47 genes (Jul 2025); HLA-B >7,000 alleles vs ≈6,000 each for HLA-A and HLA-C (Dec 2020 release); six classical genes = 87.3% of named alleles; extended MHC >7 Mb at 6p21.3 with >420 genes. Bw6 ≈2/3 and Bw4 ≈1/3 of HLA-B alleles; epitope residues at positions 77–83; Bw4-associated epitope defined by 82L or 83R in the α1 domain. Crossmatch: current-serum CDC positive with IgG class I DSA = high risk, hyperacute rejection, veto; historic-serum positive graded by antibody class and specificity; serum older than 6 months cannot predict the crossmatch, so a virtual crossmatch needs a sample from the last 3–6 months.
explanation.differs: Public vs private epitope; Bw4 (≈1/3 of HLA-B alleles, also on A23/A24/A25/A32, NKB1 ligand) vs Bw6 (≈2/3, HLA-B only, invariant at 77–83 except B*73:01); current vs historic serum; broad bead pattern from one public-epitope antibody vs genuinely multiple specificities.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: decide whether an old positive crossmatch blocks transplantation, interpret a wide single-antigen-bead pattern as one public-epitope antibody, name the most polymorphic HLA locus, and recognise that Bw4 is not confined to HLA-B.

mnemonic.text: B is the BIGGEST BOOK — HLA-B has more named alleles than any other HLA gene. Bw4 and Bw6 are the COVER whole families of antigens share, so one antibody reads every copy. And only TODAY’S serum can veto the transplant.
mnemonic.explanation: Ties the most polymorphic locus, the public-epitope idea behind broad bead patterns, and the serum-timing rule into one image.
mnemonic.limitation: The biggest-book ranking is a snapshot of a database that grows every quarter, and allele counts are not the same as functional diversity; the shared-cover image hides that Bw4 is also carried by some HLA-A antigens while Bw6 is HLA-B only; and “only today’s serum” does not mean a historical positive is harmless, because it is still graded as immunological risk.

analogyLimitations: The opening case is invented; the bead pattern, serum dates and crossmatch results are illustrative.
Allele counts are database snapshots that change with each quarterly release.
Crossmatch risk grading follows published UK and European frameworks; local acceptance policy varies by programme.
Visuals are schematic cards, not real bead histograms or biopsy images.

questions.stem: A renal transplant candidate has a positive T-cell CDC crossmatch recorded on a serum drawn three years ago, and a negative CDC crossmatch on today’s serum against the current donor. How should the historic positive be handled?

options.text: It is graded as immunological risk by antibody class and specificity, but is not by itself a veto when the current crossmatch is negative
options.rationale: Correct. Published risk frameworks grade historic positives by antibody class and specificity, and a historic positive did not significantly affect outcome when the fresh-serum crossmatch was negative.

options.text: It is an absolute contraindication, identical to a current-serum positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only the positive crossmatch on current serum carries the hyperacute-rejection veto; every positive was treated as a contraindication historically, but that changed.

options.text: It can be ignored entirely because only today’s serum matters
options.rationale: Incorrect. A historic positive still raises immunological risk, including the risk of an anamnestic response, and changes immunosuppression planning.

options.text: It means the current crossmatch must be repeated with the three-year-old serum as the only valid sample
options.rationale: Incorrect. A serum older than six months cannot predict the crossmatch; a current sample, within roughly three to six months, is required.

questions.stem: A single-antigen-bead panel is positive for a long list of HLA-B antigens together with HLA-A23 and A24. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A single antibody directed at the Bw4 public epitope, which is shared across many HLA-B antigens and some HLA-A antigens
options.rationale: Correct. A public epitope is shared by many antigens, so one antibody turns every bead carrying it positive; Bw4 is carried by HLA-B alleles and by A23, A24, A25 and A32.

options.text: Roughly twenty separate alloantibodies, one per positive bead
options.rationale: Incorrect. Broad bead patterns are usually one antibody against a shared epitope, which is what classical cross-reactive groups describe.

options.text: An antibody to a private epitope
options.rationale: Incorrect. A private epitope is found on one antigen only and gives a narrow pattern.

options.text: Contamination, because Bw4 cannot appear on HLA-A antigens
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bw4 is found on HLA-B and on some HLA-A antigens; only Bw6 is restricted to HLA-B.

questions.stem: Which statement about HLA polymorphism is correct?

options.text: HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene, and the total number of named HLA alleles rises with every database release
options.rationale: Correct. HLA-B had more than 7,000 named alleles against about 6,000 each for HLA-A and HLA-C in the December 2020 release, and the database grew from over 25,000 alleles in October 2019 to more than 43,000 by July 2025.

options.text: HLA-C is the most polymorphic HLA gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. HLA-C carries fewer named alleles than HLA-B.

options.text: The number of named HLA alleles has been fixed since 2019
options.rationale: Incorrect. Named alleles rose from over 25,000 in October 2019 to more than 43,000 by July 2025.

options.text: The classical loci HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQB1 and -DPB1 hold only a small minority of named alleles
options.rationale: Incorrect. Those six genes account for 87.3% of alleles in the database.

claims.text: HLA-B is the most polymorphic HLA gene; per-locus and database-wide allele counts and their growth; MHC span and gene content; six classical genes hold 87.3% of alleles.

Bw4 and Bw6 are mutually exclusive serological epitopes on HLA-B defined by residues 77–83, Bw6 on about two-thirds and Bw4 on about one-third of HLA-B alleles; Bw6 is HLA-B only (B*73:01 excepted) while Bw4 is also carried by HLA-A23, A24, A25 and A32; the Bw4-associated epitope is defined by 82L or 83R in the α1 domain; Bw4 is an NKB1 ligand.

Public epitopes are shared by two or more antigens and private epitopes by one; classical CREG cross-reactivity is an antibody binding a public epitope, so one specificity produces a broad single-antigen-bead pattern.
Anti-Bw4 donor-specific antibody can cause rapid C4d-positive antibody-mediated rejection even in a recipient graded low risk before transplant.

A positive CDC crossmatch on current recipient serum with IgG class I DSA is high risk and a veto to transplantation; a positive crossmatch on historical serum is graded by antibody class and specificity and did not significantly affect outcome when the fresh-serum crossmatch was negative; sera older than six months cannot predict a crossmatch, so a virtual crossmatch needs a sample from within three to six months.
Reviewer Hit 14’s claim that 80–90% of posttransplant kidney-recipient alloantibodies target CREG determinants.

claims.text: Opening scenario with its serum dates, bead pattern and crossmatch results.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 50 Hit 7 and the Number Vault give 2019 counts (>6,500 HLA-B alleles, >23,000 total HLA alleles) as current. The IPD-IMGT/HLA Database held >43,000 alleles across 47 genes by July 2025 (Barker 2026), having passed >35,000 in 2022 (Barker 2023); HLA-B already exceeded 7,000 alleles in the December 2020 release (Di 2021). The lesson teaches the counts as dated snapshots of a quarterly-updated database (register flag rv-hla-allele-counts-2019).

Ch. 50 Hit 14 describes Bw4/Bw6 as a diallelic public-epitope system on HLA-B. Gumperz 1995 states that Bw6 is found only on HLA-B but Bw4 is found on HLA-B and some HLA-A alleles, and El-Awar 2017 lists the Bw4-associated epitope on A23, A24, A25 and A32. Missing this makes anti-Bw4 patterns that include HLA-A beads look like a technical error (register flag rv-bw4-also-hla-a).

Ch. 50 Hit 14 states that 80–90% of posttransplant kidney-recipient alloantibodies target CREG determinants. No open-access source read here supports that proportion; the figure traces to Rodey and colleagues (Hum Immunol 1994), which is closed access. Taught as a pending claim only (register flag rv-creg-80-90-source).

Ch. 50 Trap 6 reduces a historic-serum positive to “a risk factor for non-hyperacute graft loss”. Althaf 2017 grades a historical positive CDC (DTT) crossmatch with IgG class I or II DSA as HIGH immunological risk because of anamnestic secondary responses, and only historical positives from cross-reactive alloantibodies as intermediate risk, while Katalinić 2025 reports that a historical positive did not significantly affect outcomes when the fresh-serum crossmatch was negative. The direction of the trap is right but the grading is programme-dependent (register flag rv-historic-xm-risk-grade).

The crossmatch risk grading taught here comes from a UK-authored review (Althaf 2017) and a Croatian/Eurotransplant-framed review (Katalinić 2025). Acceptance thresholds, mandatory physical crossmatch rules and virtual-crossmatch policy are set nationally; Philippine transplant programme requirements are not covered by these sources.

morphology.note: No images; epitope distribution, bead patterns and crossmatch grading are shown as schematic cards. No real bead histograms or biopsy photomicrographs are included.

verification.notes: 5 claims checked against Barker 2026, Robinson 2020, Barker 2023, Di 2021, Arumugam 2024, Gumperz 1995, El-Awar 2017, Bang 2025, Althaf 2017 and Katalinić 2025, all read as full text from Europe PMC (Gumperz 1995 as scanned article text). 2 claims pending (the 80–90% CREG proportion, which traces to a closed-access 1994 paper, and the protein-level counts). No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
